Introduction

Aim

The aim of this assignment is to synthesise your understanding of NumPy ndarrays, visualisation with matplotlib, and object-oriented programming. You will apply these in an engineering problem, namely the analysis of an overhead power line installation similar to that shown in Figure 1. Your solutions are to be formally implemented in Python, using the functionality covered in lectures.

Learning Objectives

This assignment supports the following learning objectives, as listed in the Electronic Course Profile:

  1. Differentiate and apply program constructs such as variables, selection, iteration and sub-routines.
  2. Recognise and apply basic object-oriented design methodologies, along with associated concepts such as classes, instances and methods.
  3. Interpret an engineering problem and design an algorithmic solution to the problem.
  4. Apply techniques for program testing and debugging.
  5. Apply sound programming techniques to the solution of real world engineering problems.
  6. Analyse and visualise engineering data.

Background

Overhead power lines are central to the transmission and distribution of electrical power. In a country the size of Australia, they represent critical infrastructure that link renewable (e.g. large-scale solar PV arrays, wind turbines) and non-renewable (e.g. coal-fired turbines) sources of electricity with storage (e.g. pumped hydroelectricity) over very large distances.

The consequences of power line failure can be significant. In 2016, extreme weather contributed to the collapse of more than 20 transmission line towers (see Figure 2), which in turn resulted in a blackout in most of the state of South Australia. During cyclones and severe storms, falling trees can break power lines, leaving them live and at ground level. Inadequate clearance can result in the interaction of power lines with heavy equipment (e.g. cranes, excavators), resulting in serious injury or death. Designing a power line with adequate ground clearance is a central component of this assignment.

The characteristic shape of a power line is described by a function called a catenary curve (see Equation 1). The general form of this function is,

\[ y(x) = \text{scale} * \cosh(x / \text{scale}), \tag{1}\] where: \[\text{scale} = \text{tension} / \text{weight}\] and:

  • \(x\) is the horizontal distance along the cable which ranges from \(-span/2\) to \(span/2\)
  • \(span = x_R - x_L\) is the horizontal distance between the two poles that the cable connects to
  • \(\text{tension}\) is the tension in the cable (in Newtons)
  • \(\text{weight}\) is the weight per unit length of the cable (in Newtons per metre). Note that wherever we refer to weight in this assignment, we are referring to the weight per unit length of the cable.

Before using Equation 1 to predict the shape of a power line, it must first be scaled such that the ends match the pole coordinates \((x_L, x_R)\) and height, \(\text{height}\). These transformations result in,

\[ y(x) = \text{scale} * \cosh(x / \text{scale}) - y(x_L) + \text{height}, \]

where:

  • \(y(x_L)\) is the value of the unscaled catenary curve at \(x_L\), which can be calculated using Equation 1.
  • \(\text{height}\) is the height of the poles that the cable connects to (in metres)
  • \(x_L\) and \(x_R\) are the x coordinates of the left and right poles that the cable connects to, respectively (in metres)

The Problem

You have been provided with a file that contains data related to a short power line. It includes the ID and easting (i.e. distance in metres in the east-west direction, as measured from a reference point) of each pole. For the purposes of these tasks, you can assume that:

  • The power line is installed on perfectly flat terrain.
  • Poles are connected to one another by a single cable that is fitted to the top of the poles (which are all the same height).
  • The left pole is the pole with the smaller easting value, and the right pole is the pole with the larger easting value.

Your task is to calculate and visualise the shape of each cable in this power line and then determine the line tension required to ensure a minimum safe ground clearance. You will do these things using both procedural and object-oriented programming.

Restrictions

You must use only the libraries that we have taught you in this course: namely NumPy and matplotlib. You are not allowed to use any other libraries. If you use other libraries, then the autograder will not be able to run your code and you will receive a mark of zero for the assignment.

def raw_catenary(x_coord: float, tension: float, mass: float) -> float:

An example usage of the functionn is shown below:

x_coord = 5.0
tension = 1000.0
mass = 0.5

print(f"The y coordinate of the unscaled catenary at x = {x_coord} is: {y_coord}")

Important

For this function, x_coord is assumed to be within the range of -span/2 to span/2.

Notice that the function uses the variable mass (which represents the mass per unit length of the cable in kg/m) instead of weight in its signature. How can you calculate the weight from the mass?

Task 5 (2 marks)

Write a function determine_min_cable_tension() that determines the minimum tension required to achieve a desired clearance. The function should accept the following parameters as shown below:

def determine_min_cable_tension(left_pole: float, right_pole: float, mass: float,
                          height: float, desired_clearance: float) -> float:

An example usage of the function is shown below:

left_pole = 0.0
right_pole = 100.0
mass = 0.5
height = 10.0
desired_clearance = 9.0
min_tension = determine_min_cable_tension(left_pole, right_pole, mass,
                                   height, desired_clearance)
print(f"The minimum tension required to achieve a clearance of {desired_clearance} m is: {min_tension} N")
Output
The minimum tension required to achieve a clearance of 9.0 m is: 6132.066249847412 N
Tip

There is no analytical solution to this problem, so you will need to use a numerical method to solve it. A simple approach is to use a “guess and check” method, where you start with an initial guess for the tension and then keep on adding a small amount to the tension until you achieve the desired clearance. There are some more efficient numerical methods, but you will need to do some research to find out about them.

Part C: Representing Cables as Objects

For the rest of this assignment, we will now mostly leave behind numpy and focus on using classes to represent our cables. The functions that you wrote for previous tasks will still be of use here.

Task 9 (1 mark)

Write a class Cable that represents a cable. The class is expected to privately store the following attributes:

  • id: the id of the cable, which serves as an identifier for each cable.
  • left_pole: the x coordinate of the left pole that the cable connects to
  • right_pole: the x coordinate of the right pole that the cable connects to
  • tension: the tension of the cable
  • mass: the mass per unit length of the cable
  • height: the height of the poles that the cable connects to

The class should have the following methods:

  • __init__(self, id: str, left_pole: float, right_pole: float, tension: float, mass: float, height: float): the constructor method that initialises the attributes of the class.
  • get_left_pole(self): a getter method that returns the x coordinate of the left pole
  • get_right_pole(self): a getter method that returns the x coordinate of the right pole
  • get_tension(self): a getter method that returns the tension of the cable
  • get_mass(self): a getter method that returns the mass per unit length of the cable
  • get_height(self): a getter method that returns the height of the poles that the cable
  • get_id(self): a method that returns the id of the cable.
  • set_tension(self, tension: float): a setter method that sets the tension of the cable to a new value.

Here is an example of how the class can be used:

cable = Cable("Cable 1", 0.0, 100.0, 2500.0, 0.5, 10.0)
print(f"Cable ID: {cable.get_id()}")
print(f"Left pole x coordinate: {cable.get_left_pole()}")
print(f"Right pole x coordinate: {cable.get_right_pole()}")
print(f"Tension: {cable.get_tension()} N")
print(f"Mass per unit length: {cable.get_mass()} kg/m")
print(f"Height of poles: {cable.get_height()} m")

cable.set_tension(3000.0)
print(f"New tension: {cable.get_tension()} N")
Output
Cable ID: Cable 1
Left pole x coordinate: 0.0
Right pole x coordinate: 100.0
Tension: 2500.0 N
Mass per unit length: 0.5 kg/m
Height of poles: 10.0 m
New tension: 3000.0 N

Task 10 (2 marks)

Write the following additional methods to extend the functionality of the Cable class:

  • calc_clearance(self): a method that calculates the minimum clearance of the cable from the ground.
  • plot(self, num_points: int): a method that plots the cable using the parameters of the cable and the number of points specified. The method should also plot the poles that the cable connects to.
  • update_min_tension(self, desired_clearance: float): a method that determines the minimum tension required to achieve a desired clearance for the cable and updates the tension attribute of the cable to this new value.
  • cable_coordinates(self, num_points: int): a method that returns the x and y coordinates of the cable for the given number of points.
  • calc_span(self): a method that calculates the span of the cable.
  • calc_length(self): a method that calculates the length of the cable.
Tip

The length of the cable is defined by the following equation:

\[\text{Length} = 2 * \text{scale} * \sinh\left(\frac{\text{span}}{2 * \text{scale}}\right)\]

where \(\text{scale} = \frac{\text{tension}}{\text{weight}}\)

Here is an example of how these methods can be used:

cable = Cable("Cable 1", 0.0, 100.0, 2500.0, 0.5, 10.0)
clearance = cable.calc_clearance()
print(f"Minimum clearance from the ground: {clearance} m")

cable.update_min_tension(9.0)
print(f"Updated tension to achieve a clearance of 9.0 m: {cable.get_tension()} N")

x_coords, y_coords = cable.cable_coordinates(50)
print(f"Cable x coordinates: {x_coords}")
print(f"Cable y coordinates: {y_coords}")

span = cable.calc_span()
print(f"Span of the cable: {span} m")
length = cable.calc_length()
print(f"Length of the cable: {length} m")

cable.plot(50)

Task 12 (2 marks)

Write a class Line which stores a set of Cable objects and has the following methods:

  • __init__(self, cables: list[Cable]): the constructor method that initialises the attributes of the class.
  • get_cable(self, id: str): a method that returns the Cable object with the given id. If the id does not correspond to any cable in the line, the method should return None.
  • plot(self, num_points_cable: int): a method that plots the line of cables using the plot_cable() method of the Cable class and the number of points specified for each cable. You should ensure that each cable is labelled with its id in the plot.
  • min_line_tension(self, desired_clearance: float): a method that determines the overall minimum tension required to achieve a desired clearance for the line of cables and updates the tension of each cable in the line to this new value. This method should also return the coordinates of the poles between which the minimum clearance occurs.

An example usage of the class is shown below:

cables = create_cables("pole_data.csv", 2500.0, 0.5, 10.0)
line = Line(cables)

# grabbing the correct cable
cable = line.get_cable("Cable: 0-1")
print(f"Cable ID: {cable.get_id()}") 

tension, left_pole, right_pole = line.min_line_tension(9.0)
print(f"Minimum tension for line of poles with desired clearance of 9.0 = {tension}")
print(f"Minimum tension determined by poles {left_pole} and {right_pole}")

# this shows that the tension of the cable has been updated
cable = line.get_cable("Cable: 0-1")
print(f"Updated tension for {cable.get_id()}: {cable.get_tension()} N") 
clearance = cable.calc_clearance()
print(f"Updated clearance for {cable.get_id()}: {clearance} m")

# plotting the line of cables
line.plot(50)
Output
Cable ID: Cable: 0-1
Minimum tension for line of poles with desired clearance of 9.0 = 6132.066249847412
Minimum tension determined by poles 20210.0 and 20310.0
Updated tension for Cable: 0-1: 6132.066249847412 N
Updated clearance for Cable: 0-1: 9.750024947811653 m

Tip

When you are plotting the line of cables, you should ensure that each cable is labelled with its id in the plot. Additionally, you do not need to manually colour the cables, as you can let matplotlib automatically assign different colours to each cable.

The min_line_tension() method is a bit more complex than the determine_min_cable_tension() function you wrote for Task 5. Once you have determined the minimum tension required overall, you will then have to ensure that each cable in the line also matches this tension.

Assignment Submission

You must submit 2 files to Gradescope: a2.py and ai_statement.pdf. You will write your code solution in a2.py and you will write your usage of ai statement in ai_statement.pdf. If you do not submit ai_statement.pdf, or if the file is empty, you will automatically receive 0% for the assignment, even if your code is perfect. The autograder will clearly state whether your ai_statement.pdf is missing or empty, so make sure to carefully check the autograder results after you submit your assignment.

As such, even if you didn’t use ai for this assignment, you must declare that in your assignment statement. The layout of this statement is up to you, as it is not assessed directly. The following link is an official uq guidance on how to structure your ai statement: UQ Library
